Using determinism of aa, we check that

∎

Proposition 4.3.

𝖥𝗂𝗇𝖲𝗍𝗈𝖼𝗁\mathsf{FinStoch}, 𝖡𝗈𝗋𝖾𝗅𝖲𝗍𝗈𝖼𝗁\mathsf{BorelStoch}, 𝖦𝖺𝗎𝗌𝗌\mathsf{Gauss} and 𝖱𝖾𝗅+\mathsf{Rel}^{+} have all conditionals.

Proof.

In 𝖡𝗈𝗋𝖾𝗅𝖲𝗍𝗈𝖼𝗁\mathsf{BorelStoch}, the definition of conditionals instantiates to regular conditional distributions which are known to exist under the assumptions of the category (that is on standard Borel spaces) (see (11, 11.7), (2, Thm. 3.5)). As a special case, conditionals in 𝖥𝗂𝗇𝖲𝗍𝗈𝖼𝗁\mathsf{FinStoch} are given by the traditional conditional distribution (11, 11.2)

(19) ψ|X​(y|x)=ψ⁡(x,y)ψX​(x) when ​πX​(x)>0\psi|_{X}(y|x)=\frac{\psi(x,y)}{\psi_{X}(x)}\quad\text{ when }\pi_{X}(x)>0

Conditionals in 𝖦𝖺𝗎𝗌𝗌\mathsf{Gauss} exist and can be given using an explicit formula generalizing (6) (11, 11.8). The property that conditionals of Gaussians are again Gaussian is sometimes called self-conjugacy (24).

In 𝖱𝖾𝗅+\mathsf{Rel}^{+}, the conditional of the state R⊆X×YR\subseteq X\times Y with respect to XX is given by ‘slicing’ the relation

R|X​(x)={y∈Y:(x,y)∈R}R|_{X}(x)=\{y\in Y:(x,y)\in R\}

which is nothing but RR itself. ∎

4.2. Almost-sure Equality, Absolute Continuity and Supports

Conditionals in Markov categories are generally not uniquely determined, although there is still a sense in which they are unique. For example, the formula (19) only determines ψ|X\psi|_{X} on the set {x:π⁡(x)>0}\{x:\pi(x)>0\}, which we call the support of ψX\psi_{X}. Outside of the support, the conditional may be modified arbitrarily. Similarly, the formula for conditionals of Gaussian distributions (6) depends on a choice of generalized inverse, which is only unique on the appropriate support.

If the reader is familiar with measure-theoretic probability, they will recall that the essential uniqueness of conditionals, when they exist, is usually stated in terms of ‘almost-sure equality’ and ‘absolute continuity’. These have established generalizations to Markov categories in general, as we now recall (Definitions 4.4 and 4.7 respectively). These definitions specialize to the measure-theoretic concepts by fixing a Markov category (Propositions 4.5, 4.9), but for a reader not familiar with measure-theoretic probability, the definitions can be taken as basic. An reference of measure theoretic terminology is given in Section 8.1.

Definition 4.4 ((6, 5.1), (11, 13.1)).

Let μ:I→X\mu:I\to X be a distribution. Two morphisms f,g:X→Yf,g:X\to Y are called μ\mu-almost surely equal (written f=μgf=_{\mu}g) if

⟨𝗂𝖽X,f⟩​μ=⟨𝗂𝖽X,g⟩​μ\langle\mathsf{id}_{X},f\rangle\mu=\langle\mathsf{id}_{X},g\rangle\mu
Proposition 4.5.

For our example categories, the abstract definition of almost sure equality recovers the familiar meaning:

  1. (1)

    In 𝖥𝗂𝗇𝖲𝗍𝗈𝖼𝗁\mathsf{FinStoch}, f,g:X→D⁡(Y)f,g:X\to D(Y) are μ\mu-almost surely equal iff the distributions f⁡(x)=g⁡(x)f(x)=g(x) agree for all xx with μ⁡(x)>0\mu(x)>0

  2. (2)

    In 𝖡𝗈𝗋𝖾𝗅𝖲𝗍𝗈𝖼𝗁\mathsf{BorelStoch}, f,g:X→𝒢⁡(Y)f,g:X\to\mathcal{G}(Y) are μ\mu-almost surely equal iff f⁡(x)=g⁡(x)f(x)=g(x) as measures for μ\mu-almost all xx, that is the set {x:f⁡(x)≠g⁡(x)}\{x:f(x)\neq g(x)\} has μ\mu-measure 00.

  3. (3)

    In 𝖦𝖺𝗎𝗌𝗌\mathsf{Gauss}, if μ:I→m\mu:I\to m is a distribution with support SS(in the sense of Section 2.1), then f,g:m→nf,g:m\to n are μ\mu-almost surely equal iff f∘x=g∘xf\circ x=g\circ x for all elements x∈Sx\in S, seen as deterministic states x:0→mx:0\to m.

  4. (4)

    In 𝖱𝖾𝗅+\mathsf{Rel}^{+}, if M⊆XM\subseteq X and R,S:X→𝒫+​(Y)R,S:X\to\mathcal{P}^{+}(Y) are two left-total relations, then R=MSR=_{M}S iff R⁡(x)=S⁡(x)R(x)=S(x) for all x∈Mx\in M.

Proof.

The results for 𝖥𝗂𝗇𝖲𝗍𝗈𝖼𝗁\mathsf{FinStoch} and 𝖡𝗈𝗋𝖾𝗅𝖲𝗍𝗈𝖼𝗁\mathsf{BorelStoch} are given in (11, 13.2) and (12, 3.19). The result for 𝖦𝖺𝗎𝗌𝗌\mathsf{Gauss} is a strengthening of the result for 𝖡𝗈𝗋𝖾𝗅𝖲𝗍𝗈𝖼𝗁\mathsf{BorelStoch}. The morphisms f,g:m→nf,g:m\to n can be faithfully considered 𝖡𝗈𝗋𝖾𝗅𝖲𝗍𝗈𝖼𝗁\mathsf{BorelStoch} maps f,g:ℝm→𝒢⁡(ℝn)f,g:\mathbb{R}^{m}\to\mathcal{G}(\mathbb{R}^{n}), so we have f⁡(x)=g⁡(x)f(x)=g(x) for μ\mu-almost all xx. Because f,gf,g are furthermore continuous functions and μ\mu is equivalent to the Lebesgue measure on the support SS, the equality almost everywhere can be strengthened to equality on all of SS. ∎

It follows directly from the definitions that conditional distributions are almost surely unique:

Proposition 4.6.

If ψ:I→X⊗Y\psi:I\to X\otimes Y is a distribution and ψ|X,ψ|X′\psi|_{X},\psi|_{X}^{\prime} are two morphisms satisfying (17), then

(20) ψ|X=ψXψ|X′\psi|_{X}=_{\psi_{X}}\psi|_{X}^{\prime}

That is, conditional distributions are unique almost surely with respect to the marginal ψX\psi_{X}

The important notion of absolute continuity can now be formulated naturally in terms of almost-sure equality:

Definition 4.7 ((12, 2.8)).

Given two distributions μ,ν:I→X\mu,\nu:I\to X, we say that μ\mu is absolutely continuous with respect to ν\nu, written μ≪ν\mu\ll\nu, if for all f,g:X→Yf,g:X\to Y we have

f=νg implies f=μgf=_{\nu}g\text{ implies }f=_{\mu}g

Absolute continuity lets us strengthen statements about almost-sure equality to actual equality.

Lemma 4.8.

If μ:I→X\mu:I\to X, f=μgf=_{\mu}g and x≪μx\ll\mu then f​x=g​xfx=gx

On the other hand, ≪\ll recovers the usual notion of absolute continuity in our example categories.

Proposition 4.9.
  1. (1)

    In 𝖥𝗂𝗇𝖲𝗍𝗈𝖼𝗁\mathsf{FinStoch}, μ≪ν\mu\ll\nu iff ν⁡(x)=0\nu(x)=0 implies μ⁡(x)=0\mu(x)=0

  2. (2)

    In 𝖡𝗈𝗋𝖾𝗅𝖲𝗍𝗈𝖼𝗁\mathsf{BorelStoch}, μ≪ν\mu\ll\nu iff for all measurable sets AA, ν⁡(A)=0\nu(A)=0 implies μ⁡(A)=0\mu(A)=0

  3. (3)

    In 𝖦𝖺𝗎𝗌𝗌\mathsf{Gauss}, μ≪ν\mu\ll\nu iff 𝗌𝗎𝗉𝗉⁡(μ)⊆𝗌𝗎𝗉𝗉⁡(ν)\mathsf{supp}(\mu)\subseteq\mathsf{supp}(\nu) (in the sense of Section 2.1).

  4. (4)

    In 𝖱𝖾𝗅+\mathsf{Rel}^{+}, R≪SR\ll S iff R⊆SR\subseteq S.

Proof.

The claim for 𝖥𝗂𝗇𝖲𝗍𝗈𝖼𝗁\mathsf{FinStoch} follows immediately from Proposition 4.5, and the result for 𝖡𝗈𝗋𝖾𝗅𝖲𝗍𝗈𝖼𝗁\mathsf{BorelStoch} is given in (12, 2.9). Proposition 4.5 implies that the support condition for 𝖦𝖺𝗎𝗌𝗌\mathsf{Gauss} is sufficient. To see that it is also necessary, let x∈𝗌𝗎𝗉𝗉⁡(μ)∖𝗌𝗎𝗉𝗉⁡(ν)x\in\mathsf{supp}(\mu)\setminus\mathsf{supp}(\nu). Then we can find two affine functions f,gf,g which agree on 𝗌𝗎𝗉𝗉⁡(ν)\mathsf{supp}(\nu) but f⁡(x)≠g⁡(x)f(x)\neq g(x). Now f=νgf=_{\nu}g but not f=μgf=_{\mu}g, hence μ≪̸ν\mu\not\ll\nu. ∎

In 𝖥𝗂𝗇𝖲𝗍𝗈𝖼𝗁\mathsf{FinStoch}, we can also rephrase μ≪ν\mu\ll\nu as 𝗌𝗎𝗉𝗉⁡(μ)⊆𝗌𝗎𝗉𝗉⁡(ν)\mathsf{supp}(\mu)\subseteq\mathsf{supp}(\nu) if we define 𝗌𝗎𝗉𝗉⁡(μ)={x:μ⁡(x)>0}\mathsf{supp}(\mu)=\{x:\mu(x)>0\}. For the purposes of our development, it will suffice to consider the special case of the absolute continuity relation restricted to deterministic states and distributions. We take this as the categorical definition of supports:

Definition 4.10.

If x:I→Xx:I\to X is a deterministic state, we say that xx lies in the support of μ\mu if x≪μx\ll\mu.

We obtain the following characterization

Proposition 4.11.
  1. (1)

    In 𝖥𝗂𝗇𝖲𝗍𝗈𝖼𝗁\mathsf{FinStoch}, x≪μx\ll\mu iff μ⁡(x)>0\mu(x)>0

  2. (2)

    In 𝖡𝗈𝗋𝖾𝗅𝖲𝗍𝗈𝖼𝗁\mathsf{BorelStoch}, x≪μx\ll\mu iff μ⁡({x})>0\mu(\{x\})>0

  3. (3)

    In 𝖦𝖺𝗎𝗌𝗌\mathsf{Gauss}, x≪μx\ll\mu iff x∈𝗌𝗎𝗉𝗉⁡(μ)x\in\mathsf{supp}(\mu)

  4. (4)

    In 𝖱𝖾𝗅+\mathsf{Rel}^{+}, x≪Rx\ll R if x∈Rx\in R

It is crucial that the support of a distribution can change with the surrounding Markov category:

Example 4.12.

Let μ=𝒩⁡(0,1)\mu=\mathcal{N}(0,1) be the standard normal distribution. When considered in 𝖦𝖺𝗎𝗌𝗌\mathsf{Gauss}, its support is ℝ\mathbb{R} and in particular for all x0∈ℝx_{0}\in\mathbb{R} we have x0≪μx_{0}\ll\mu. In 𝖡𝗈𝗋𝖾𝗅𝖲𝗍𝗈𝖼𝗁\mathsf{BorelStoch}, we have x0≪̸μx_{0}\not\ll\mu because μ⁡({x0})=0\mu(\{x_{0}\})=0.

This means that smaller Markov categories like 𝖦𝖺𝗎𝗌𝗌\mathsf{Gauss} have a stronger notion of support, which in turn allows more interesting conditions to be evaluated. This is reminiscent of the tradeoff between expressiveness and well-behavedness discussed under the notion of “well-behaved disintegrations” in (42).

By combining the notions of conditionals and support, we can now present an abstract theory of inference problems.

4.3. Abstract Inference Problems

Let ℂ\mathbb{C} be a Markov category with all conditionals. In order to describe statistical inference categorically, we introduce the following terminology:

  1. (1)

    An observation is a constant piece of data, that is a deterministic state o:I→Ko:I\to K.

  2. (2)

    An inference problem over XX is a tuple (K,ψ,o)(K,\psi,o) of an object KK, a joint distribution ψ:I→X⊗K\psi:I\to X\otimes K called the model and an observation o:I→Ko:I\to K.

The problem is then to infer the posterior distribution over XX conditioned on the observation oo. An inference problem can either succeed, or fail if the observation oo is inconsistent with the model.

  1. (1)

    We say (K,ψ,o)(K,\psi,o) succeeds if the observation lies in the support of the model, i.e. o≪ψKo\ll\psi_{K}. In that case, a solution to the inference problem is the composite ψ|K∘o:I→X\psi|_{K}\circ o:I\to X where ψ|K:K→X\psi|_{K}:K\to X is a conditional to ψ\psi with respect to KK. The solution is also referred to as a posterior for the problem.

  2. (2)

    If o≪̸ψKo\not\ll\psi_{K}, we say that the inference problem fails or is infeasible.

Proposition 4.13.

Solutions to inference problems are unique, i.e. if (K,ψ,o)(K,\psi,o) succeeds and ψ|K,ψ|K′\psi|_{K},\psi|_{K}^{\prime} are two conditionals then ψ|K​(o)=ψ|K′​(o)\psi|_{K}(o)=\psi|_{K}^{\prime}(o).

Proof.

Combine Lemma 4.8 and Proposition 4.6. ∎

Definition 4.14.

We call two inference problems observationally equivalent if they either both fail, or they both succeed with equal posteriors.

For the rest of this section, we will rederive Example 2.1 in terms of the categorical machinery and show that it matches the conditioning procedure from Section 2.

Example 4.15.

The example 2.1 can be written as

X\displaystyle X ∼𝒩⁡(0,1)\displaystyle\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)
Y\displaystyle Y ∼𝒩⁡(0,1)\displaystyle\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)
(X−Y)\displaystyle(X-Y)\, :=  0\displaystyle{:}\scalebox{0.5}[1]{${=}$}\,\,0

which corresponds to the inference problem (1,μ,0)(1,\mu,0) where μ:0→2⊗1\mu:0\to 2\otimes 1 has covariance matrix

Σ=(10101−11−12)\Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&1\\ 0&1&-1\\ 1&-1&2\end{pmatrix}

A conditional with respect to the third coordinate ZZ is

μ|Z​(z)=(0.50.5)​z+𝒩​(0.50.50.50.5)\mu|_{Z}(z)=\begin{pmatrix}0.5\\ 0.5\end{pmatrix}z+\mathcal{N}\begin{pmatrix}0.5&0.5\\ 0.5&0.5\end{pmatrix}

which can be verified by calculating (17). The marginal μZ=𝒩⁡(2)\mu_{Z}=\mathcal{N}(2) is supported on all of ℝ\mathbb{R}, hence 0≪μZ0\ll\mu_{Z} and by Proposition 4.13 the composite

μ|Z​(0)=𝒩​(0.50.50.50.5)\mu|_{Z}(0)=\mathcal{N}\begin{pmatrix}0.5&0.5\\ 0.5&0.5\end{pmatrix}

is the uniquely defined solution to the inference problem.

The same inference problem would not have a solution when interpreted in 𝖡𝗈𝗋𝖾𝗅𝖲𝗍𝗈𝖼𝗁\mathsf{BorelStoch} instead of 𝖦𝖺𝗎𝗌𝗌\mathsf{Gauss}. This is because 0≪̸μZ0\not\ll\mu_{Z} (Example 4.12). In 𝖡𝗈𝗋𝖾𝗅𝖲𝗍𝗈𝖼𝗁\mathsf{BorelStoch}, we can only condition on observations of positive probability; this agrees with the classical definition of conditional probability

P⁡(A|B)=defP⁡(A∩B)P⁡(B)​ if ​P​(B)>0P(A|B)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{def}}}{{=}}\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}\text{ if }P(B)>0

In 𝖦𝖺𝗎𝗌𝗌\mathsf{Gauss}, we can also condition on probability zero observations in a principled way because the notion of support is better behaved.

5. Compositional Conditioning – The Cond Construction

In Section 4 we have seen that Markov categories with conditionals allow a general recipe for conditioning. In order to give compositional semantics to a language with conditioning, we need to internalize the conditioning operation as a morphism. The key step is to move from a closed inference problem (K,ψ:I→X⊗K,o:I→K)(K,\psi\colon I\to X\otimes K,o\colon I\to K), to open inference problems or conditioning channels, where ψ\psi is replaced with a morphism with more general domain, so that it can be composed.

With some care, we can turn these conditioning channels into a CD-category (Definition 3.1, a monoidal category where every object has a comonoid structure). This allows us to give a denotational semantics to a CD calculus with conditioning, and in particular a denotational semantics for the Gaussian language with conditioning of Section 2. Looking forward, in Section 6 we will show that this denotational semantics is fully abstract: it precisely captures the contextual equivalence from the operational semantics.

The construction presented in this chapter is rather involved, but its well-definedness and properties are the central technical contribution of this article. From Section 5.3 onwards, we can harness the good properties the construction enjoys to return to a higher level picture and use string diagrams for studying a graphical language of conditioning.

Let ℂ\mathbb{C} be a Markov category, then a conditioning channel X↝YX\leadsto Y is given by a morphism X→Y⊗KX\to Y\otimes K together with an observation (i.e. deterministic state) o:I→Ko:I\to K. This represents an intensional open program of the form

(21) x:X⊢𝗅𝖾𝗍(y,k):Y⊗K=f(x)𝗂𝗇(k:=o);yx:X\vdash\mathsf{let}\,(y,k):Y\otimes K\,=\,f(x)\,\mathsf{in}\,{(k{:}\scalebox{0.5}[1]{${=}$}\,o);y}

We think of KK as an additional hidden output wire, to which we attach the observation oo. Such programs compose in the obvious way, by aggregating observations (Figure 7). Two representations (21) are deemed equivalent if they contextually equivalent, that is roughly they compute the same posteriors in all contexts.

An important caveat is that the primary operation we formalize is that of an exact observation (:=o)({:}\scalebox{0.5}[1]{${=}$}\,o) where oo is a deterministic state. Binary exact conditioning (=:=)(\mathrel{\scalebox{0.4}[1]{${=}$}{:}{\scalebox{0.4}[1]{${=}$}}}) between two expressions may be encoded in terms of (:=)({:}\scalebox{0.5}[1]{${=}$}\,), for example as (x==y):=true(x==y){:}\scalebox{0.5}[1]{${=}$}\,\mathrm{true} for finite sets or as (x−y):= 0(x-y){:}\scalebox{0.5}[1]{${=}$}\,0 for Gaussians. Generally, the choice of encoding does matter (Example 2.2), so we consider this choice additional structure and focus on formalizing (:=)({:}\scalebox{0.5}[1]{${=}$}\,).

For modularity, we present the construction in two stages: In the first stage (Section 5.1) we form a category 𝖮𝖻𝗌⁡(ℂ)\mathsf{Obs}(\mathbb{C}) on the same objects as ℂ\mathbb{C} consisting of the data (21) but without any quotienting. This adds, purely formally, for every observation o:I→Xo:I\to X an observation effect (:=o):X↝I({:}\scalebox{0.5}[1]{${=}$}\,o):X\leadsto I. In the second stage (Section 5.2) – this is the core of the construction – we relate these morphisms to the conditionals present in ℂ\mathbb{C}, that is we quotient by contextual equivalence. The resulting quotient is called 𝖢𝗈𝗇𝖽⁡(ℂ)\mathsf{Cond}(\mathbb{C}). Under mild assumptions, this will have the good properties of a CD category, showing that conditioning stays commutative. We demonstrate the resulting reasoning methods in Section 5.3 and Section 5.4.

5.1. Obs – Open Programs with Observations

For ease of notation, we will assume ℂ\mathbb{C} is a strictly monoidal category, that is all associators and unitors are identities (this poses no restriction by (11, 10.17)). We note that all constructions can instead be performed purely string-diagrammatically.

Definition 5.1.

The following data define a symmetric premonoidal category called 𝖮𝖻𝗌⁡(ℂ)\mathsf{Obs}(\mathbb{C}):

  • •

    the object part of 𝖮𝖻𝗌⁡(ℂ)\mathsf{Obs}(\mathbb{C}) is the same as ℂ\mathbb{C}

  • •

    morphisms X↝YX\leadsto Y are tuples (K,f,o)(K,f,o) where KK is an object of ℂ\mathbb{C}, f∈ℂ⁡(X,Y⊗K)f\in\mathbb{C}(X,Y\otimes K) and o∈ℂdet​(I,K)o\in\mathbb{C}_{\mathrm{det}}(I,K), representing (21)

  • •

    The identity on XX is IdX=(I,𝗂𝖽X,!)\mathrm{Id}_{X}=(I,\mathsf{id}_{X},!) where !=𝗂𝖽I!=\mathsf{id}_{I}.

  • •

    Composition is defined by

    (K′,f′,o′)∙(K,f,o)=(K′⊗K,(f′⊗𝗂𝖽K)​f,o′⊗o).(K^{\prime},f^{\prime},o^{\prime})\bullet(K,f,o)=(K^{\prime}\otimes K,(f^{\prime}\otimes\mathsf{id}_{K})f,o^{\prime}\otimes o).
  • •

    if (K,f,o):X↝Y(K,f,o):X\leadsto Y and (K′,f′,o′):X′↝Y′(K^{\prime},f^{\prime},o^{\prime}):X^{\prime}\leadsto Y^{\prime}, their (premonoidal) tensor product is defined as

    (K′⊗K,(𝗂𝖽Y′⊗𝗌𝗐𝖺𝗉K′,Y⊗𝗂𝖽K)​(f′⊗f),o′⊗o)(K^{\prime}\otimes K,(\mathsf{id}_{Y^{\prime}}\otimes\mathsf{swap}_{K^{\prime},Y}\otimes\mathsf{id}_{K})(f^{\prime}\otimes f),o^{\prime}\otimes o)
  • •

    There is an identity-on-objects functor J:ℂ→𝖮𝖻𝗌⁡(ℂ)J:\mathbb{C}\to\mathsf{Obs}(\mathbb{C}) that sends f:X→Yf:X\to Y to (I,f,!):X↝Y(I,f,!):X\leadsto Y. This functor is strict premonoidal and its image central

  • •

    𝖮𝖻𝗌⁡(ℂ)\mathsf{Obs}(\mathbb{C}) inherits symmetry and comonoid structure

Recall that a symmetric premonoidal category (due to (39)) is like a symmetric monoidal category where the interchange law (f1⊗f2)∘(g1⊗g2)=f1​g1⊗f2​g2(f_{1}\otimes f_{2})\circ(g_{1}\otimes g_{2})=f_{1}g_{1}\otimes f_{2}g_{2} need not hold. This is the case because 𝖮𝖻𝗌⁡(ℂ)\mathsf{Obs}(\mathbb{C}) does not yet identify observations arriving in different order. This will be remedied automatically later when passing to the quotient 𝖢𝗈𝗇𝖽⁡(ℂ)\mathsf{Cond}(\mathbb{C}). For an observation o:I→Ko:I\to K, the conditioning effect (:=o):K↝I({:}\scalebox{0.5}[1]{${=}$}\,o):K\leadsto I is defined by (I,𝗂𝖽K,o)(I,\mathsf{id}_{K},o).

Notation:

A morphism F:X↝YF:X\leadsto Y in 𝖮𝖻𝗌⁡(ℂ)\mathsf{Obs}(\mathbb{C}) consists of a morphism f:X→Y⊗Kf:X\to Y\otimes K in ℂ\mathbb{C} with an extra datum o:I→Ko:I\to K. It can be convenient to describe morphisms in 𝖮𝖻𝗌⁡(ℂ)\mathsf{Obs}(\mathbb{C}) by their underlying morphisms in ℂ\mathbb{C}, with extra ‘conditioning wires’ into the object KK and observations attached to them. Informally, we will highlight these wires dashed and blue, simply to distinguish the codomain object YY from the condition object KK. Using this notation, composition and tensor in 𝖮𝖻𝗌⁡(ℂ)\mathsf{Obs}(\mathbb{C}) take the form shown in Figure 7. In Section 5.3, we will use actual string diagram in 𝖢𝗈𝗇𝖽⁡(ℂ)\mathsf{Cond}(\mathbb{C}) as opposed to string diagrams in ℂ\mathbb{C}, which will obviate the need for blue wires.

5.2. Cond – Contextual Equivalence of Inference Programs

Let us now assume that ℂ\mathbb{C} has all conditionals. We wish to quotient 𝖮𝖻𝗌\mathsf{Obs}-morphisms by contextual equivalence, relating them to the conditionals which can be computed in ℂ\mathbb{C}. We know how to interpret closed programs, because a state (K,ψ,o):I↝X(K,\psi,o):I\leadsto X is precisely an inference problem as in Section 3: If o≪̸ψKo\not\ll\psi_{K}, the observation does not lie in the support of the model and conditioning fails. If not, we form the conditional ψ|K\psi|_{K} in ℂ\mathbb{C} and obtain a well-defined posterior μ|K∘o\mu|_{K}\circ o.

The observational equivalence (Definition 4.14) defines an equivalence relation on states I↝XI\leadsto X in 𝖢𝗈𝗇𝖽⁡(ℂ)\mathsf{Cond}(\mathbb{C}). We will extend this relation to a congruence on arbitrary morphisms X↝YX\leadsto Y by a general categorical construction.

Definition 5.2.

Given two states I↝XI\leadsto X we define (K,ψ,o)∼(K′,ψ′,o′)(K,\psi,o)\sim(K^{\prime},\psi^{\prime},o^{\prime}) if they are observationally equivalent as inference problems, that is either

  1. (1)

    o≪ψKo\ll\psi_{K} and o′≪ψK′′o^{\prime}\ll\psi^{\prime}_{K^{\prime}} and ψ|K​(o)=ψ′|K′​(o′)\psi|_{K}(o)=\psi^{\prime}|_{K^{\prime}}(o^{\prime}).

  2. (2)

    o≪̸ψKo\not\ll\psi_{K} and o′≪̸ψK′′o^{\prime}\not\ll\psi^{\prime}_{K^{\prime}}

We now give a general recipe to extend an equivalence relation on states to a congruence on arbitrary morphisms f:X→Yf:X\to Y.

Definition 5.3.

Let 𝕏\mathbb{X} be a symmetric premonoidal category. An equivalence relation ∼\sim on states 𝕏⁡(I,−)\mathbb{X}(I,-) is called functorial if ψ∼ψ′\psi\sim\psi^{\prime} implies f​ψ∼f​ψ′f\psi\sim f\psi^{\prime}. We can extend such a relation to a congruence ≈\approx on all morphisms X→YX\to Y via

f≈g⇔∀A,ψ:I→A⊗X,(𝗂𝖽A⊗f)​ψ∼(𝗂𝖽A⊗g)​ψ.f\approx g\Leftrightarrow\forall A,\psi:I\to A\otimes X,(\mathsf{id}_{A}\otimes f)\psi\sim(\mathsf{id}_{A}\otimes g)\psi.

The quotient category 𝕏/≈\mathbb{X}/{\approx} is symmetric premonoidal.

We show now that under good assumptions, the quotient by conditioning (Definition 5.2) on 𝕏=𝖮𝖻𝗌⁡(ℂ)\mathbb{X}=\mathsf{Obs}(\mathbb{C}) is functorial, and induces a quotient category 𝖢𝗈𝗇𝖽⁡(ℂ)\mathsf{Cond}(\mathbb{C}). The technical condition is that supports interact well with dataflow:

Definition 5.4.

A Markov category ℂ\mathbb{C} has precise supports if the following are equivalent for all deterministic x:I→Xx:I\to X, y:I→Yy:I\to Y, and arbitrary f:X→Yf:X\to Y and μ:I→X\mu:I\to X.

  1. (1)

    x⊗y≪⟨𝗂𝖽X,f⟩​μx\otimes y\ll\langle\mathsf{id}_{X},f\rangle\mu

  2. (2)

    x≪μx\ll\mu and y≪f​xy\ll fx

The word ‘support’ here refers to Definition 4.10.

Proposition 5.5.

𝖦𝖺𝗎𝗌𝗌\mathsf{Gauss}, 𝖥𝗂𝗇𝖲𝗍𝗈𝖼𝗁\mathsf{FinStoch}, 𝖡𝗈𝗋𝖾𝗅𝖲𝗍𝗈𝖼𝗁\mathsf{BorelStoch} and 𝖱𝖾𝗅+\mathsf{Rel}^{+} have precise supports.

Proof.

This follows from the characterizations of ≪\ll in Proposition 4.11. For 𝖦𝖺𝗎𝗌𝗌\mathsf{Gauss}, let μ\mu have support SS and f⁡(x)=A​x+𝒩⁡(b,Σ)f(x)=Ax+\mathcal{N}(b,\Sigma). Let TT be the support of 𝒩⁡(b,Σ)\mathcal{N}(b,\Sigma). The support of ⟨𝗂𝖽,f⟩​μ\langle\mathsf{id},f\rangle\mu is the image space {(x,Ax+c):x∈S,c∈T}\{(x,Ax+c):x\in S,c\in T\}. Hence (x,y)≪⟨𝗂𝖽,f⟩​μ(x,y)\ll\langle\mathsf{id},f\rangle\mu iff x≪μx\ll\mu and y≪f​xy\ll fx. Similarly, for 𝖱𝖾𝗅+\mathsf{Rel}^{+}, we readily verify

x∈{(x,y):x∈μ,(x,y)∈f}⇔x∈μ∧y∈f(x)x\in\{(x,y):x\in\mu,(x,y)\in f\}\Leftrightarrow x\in\mu\wedge y\in f(x)

For 𝖥𝗂𝗇𝖲𝗍𝗈𝖼𝗁\mathsf{FinStoch}, an outcome (x,y)(x,y) has positive probability under ⟨𝗂𝖽,f⟩​μ\langle\mathsf{id},f\rangle\mu iff xx has positive probability under μ\mu, and yy has positive probability under f(−|x)f(-|x).

For 𝖡𝗈𝗋𝖾𝗅𝖲𝗍𝗈𝖼𝗁\mathsf{BorelStoch}, the measure ψ=⟨𝗂𝖽,f⟩​μ\psi=\langle\mathsf{id},f\rangle\mu is given by

ψ⁡(A×B)=∫x∈Af⁡(B|x)​μ​(𝑑x)\psi(A\times B)=\int_{x\in A}f(B|x)\mu(\mathrm{d}x)

Hence ψ⁡({(x0,y0)})=f⁡({y0}|x)​μ​({x})\psi(\{(x_{0},y_{0})\})=f(\{y_{0}\}|x)\mu(\{x\}), which is positive exactly if μ⁡({x0})>0\mu(\{x_{0}\})>0 and f⁡({y0}|x)>0f(\{y_{0}\}|x)>0. ∎

Theorem 5.6.

Let ℂ\mathbb{C} be a Markov category that has conditionals and precise supports. Then ∼\sim is a functorial equivalence relation on 𝖮𝖻𝗌⁡(ℂ)\mathsf{Obs}(\mathbb{C}).

Proof.

Let (K,ψ,o)∼(K′,ψ′,o′):I↝X(K,\psi,o)\sim(K^{\prime},\psi^{\prime},o^{\prime}):I\leadsto X be equivalent states and (H,f,v):X↝Y(H,f,v):X\leadsto Y be any morphism. We need to show that the composites

(22) (H⊗K,(f⊗𝗂𝖽K)​ψ,v⊗o)∼(H⊗K′,(f⊗𝗂𝖽K′)​ψ′,v⊗o′)(H\otimes K,(f\otimes\mathsf{id}_{K})\psi,v\otimes o)\sim(H\otimes K^{\prime},(f\otimes\mathsf{id}_{K^{\prime}})\psi^{\prime},v\otimes o^{\prime})

are equivalent. We analyze different cases.

The states fail

If a state (K,ψ,o)(K,\psi,o) fails because o≪̸ψKo\not\ll\psi_{K}, then any composite must fail too. So both sides of (22) fail and are thus equivalent.

The composite fails

Assume from now that the states succeed and thus also have equal posteriors

(23) ψ|K​(o)=ψ′|K​(o′)\psi|_{K}(o)=\psi^{\prime}|_{K}(o^{\prime})

We first show that the success conditions on both sides of (22) are the same, so if the LHS fails so does the RHS. The “precise supports” axiom lets us split the success condition into two statements; that is the following are equivalent (and analogous for ψ′,o′\psi^{\prime},o^{\prime}):

  1. (1)

    v⊗o≪(fH⊗𝗂𝖽K)​ψv\otimes o\ll(f_{H}\otimes\mathsf{id}_{K})\psi

  2. (2)

    o≪ψKo\ll\psi_{K} and v≪fH​ψ|K​(o)v\ll f_{H}\psi|_{K}(o)

To see this, we instantiate Definition 5.4 with the morphisms μ=ψK\mu=\psi_{K} and g=fH∘ψ|Kg=f_{H}\circ\psi|_{K}, because the definition of the conditional ψ|K\psi|_{K} lets us recover

⟨g,𝗂𝖽K⟩​μ=(fH⊗𝗂𝖽K)​ψ.\langle g,\mathsf{id}_{K}\rangle\mu=(f_{H}\otimes\mathsf{id}_{K})\psi.

It is clear that condition 2 agrees for both sides of (22). Hence so does 1.

This requires the fact that isomorphisms are deterministic in a Markov category with conditionals (11, 11.26). The proof more generally works if α\alpha is deterministic and split monic. ∎

We can now give the Cond construction by means of quotienting 𝖮𝖻𝗌⁡(ℂ)\mathsf{Obs}(\mathbb{C}) modulo contextual equivalence.

Definition 5.9.

Let ℂ\mathbb{C} be a Markov category that has conditionals and precise supports. We define 𝖢𝗈𝗇𝖽⁡(ℂ)\mathsf{Cond}(\mathbb{C}) as the quotient category

𝖢𝗈𝗇𝖽(ℂ)=𝖮𝖻𝗌(ℂ)/≈\mathsf{Cond}(\mathbb{C})=\mathsf{Obs}(\mathbb{C})/{\approx}

This quotient is a CD category, and the functor J:ℂ→𝖢𝗈𝗇𝖽⁡(ℂ)J:\mathbb{C}\to\mathsf{Cond}(\mathbb{C}) preserves CD structure.

5.3. Laws for Conditioning

We will now establish convenient properties of 𝖢𝗈𝗇𝖽⁡(ℂ)\mathsf{Cond}(\mathbb{C}) in a purely abstract way. In terms of the internal language, those are the desired program equations for a language with exact conditioning. For example, the fact that 𝖢𝗈𝗇𝖽⁡(ℂ)\mathsf{Cond}(\mathbb{C}) is a well-defined CD category already implies that commutativity equation holds for such programs (Proposition 3.15).

Secondly, we can draw string diagrams in the category 𝖢𝗈𝗇𝖽⁡(ℂ)\mathsf{Cond}(\mathbb{C}). 6. Denotational Semantics and Contextual Equivalence

In Section 5 we introduced the 𝖢𝗈𝗇𝖽\mathsf{Cond} construction (Definition 5.9) as a way of building a category that accommodates the abstract inference for Markov categories (Section 4). As we have seen, we can interpret the CD calculus (Section 3) in categories built from the 𝖢𝗈𝗇𝖽\mathsf{Cond} construction, and this forms a probabilistic programming language with exact conditioning. In this final section, we will work out in detail what the 𝖢𝗈𝗇𝖽\mathsf{Cond} construction does when applied to our specific example settings of finite and Gaussian probability.

In Section 6.1, we show that the Gaussian language (Section 2) has fully abstract denotational semantics in 𝖢𝗈𝗇𝖽⁡(𝖦𝖺𝗎𝗌𝗌)\mathsf{Cond}(\mathsf{Gauss}): equality in the category coincides with the operational contextual equivalence from Section 2.3.

In Section 6.2, we conduct the same analysis for finite probability and show that 𝖢𝗈𝗇𝖽⁡(𝖥𝗂𝗇𝖲𝗍𝗈𝖼𝗁)\mathsf{Cond}(\mathsf{FinStoch}) consists of substochastic kernels up to automatic normalization. In Section 6.3, we spell out the relationship between the admissibility of automatic normalization and the expressibility of branching in the language.

6.1. Full Abstraction for the Gaussian Language

The Gaussian language embeds into the internal language of 𝖢𝗈𝗇𝖽⁡(𝖦𝖺𝗎𝗌𝗌)\mathsf{Cond}(\mathsf{Gauss}), where x=:=yx\mathrel{\scalebox{0.4}[1]{${=}$}{:}{\scalebox{0.4}[1]{${=}$}}}y is translated as (x−y):= 0(x-y){:}\scalebox{0.5}[1]{${=}$}\,0. 6.2. Contextual Equivalence for Finite Probability

With programs over a finite domain, we can understand conditioning in terms of rejection sampling. This means that we run a program NN times, with different random choices each time. We reject those runs that violate the conditions, and then we resample from the among the acceptable results. As N→∞N\to\infty, this random distribution converges to the probability distribution that the program describes.

The following reformulation is semantically equivalent: For a closed program, suppose the program would return some value x1x_{1} with probability p1p_{1}, value x2x_{2} with probability p2p_{2}, and so on. Then the probability that the program will not fail is Z=∑ipiZ=\sum_{i}p_{i}. The result of rejection sampling is a program that actually returns xix_{i} with probability piZ\frac{p_{i}}{Z}, so that we have a normalized probability distribution over {x1​…​xn}\{x_{1}\dots x_{n}\}, i.e. ∑piZ=1\sum\frac{p_{i}}{Z}=1. The quantity ZZ is called the normalization constant of the program, or sometimes model evidence.

For example, the program

𝗅𝖾𝗍x=𝖻𝖾𝗋𝗇𝗈𝗎𝗅𝗅𝗂(0.4)𝗂𝗇𝗅𝖾𝗍y=𝖻𝖾𝗋𝗇𝗈𝗎𝗅𝗅𝗂(0.4)𝗂𝗇x=:=y;x\mathsf{let}\,x\,=\,\mathsf{bernoulli}(0.4)\,\mathsf{in}\,{\mathsf{let}\,y\,=\,\mathsf{bernoulli}(0.4)\,\mathsf{in}\,{x\mathrel{\scalebox{0.4}[1]{${=}$}{:}{\scalebox{0.4}[1]{${=}$}}}y;x}}

will fail the condition with probability 2⋅0.4⋅0.6=0.482\cdot 0.4\cdot 0.6=0.48, return true with probability 0.42=0.160.4^{2}=0.16, and return false with probability 0.62=0.360.6^{2}=0.36. Under rejection sampling, once we renormalize, the program is equivalent to 𝖻𝖾𝗋𝗇𝗈𝗎𝗅𝗅𝗂⁡(0.160.36)≈𝖻𝖾𝗋𝗇𝗈𝗎𝗅𝗅𝗂⁡(0.44)\mathsf{bernoulli}(\frac{0.16}{0.36})\approx\mathsf{bernoulli}(0.44).

Rejection sampling makes sense for closed programs. For programs with free variables, we can still understand a program that rejects runs that violate the conditions, but normalization is more subtle. For example, in the program

(31) 𝗅𝖾𝗍y=𝖻𝖾𝗋𝗇𝗈𝗎𝗅𝗅𝗂(0.4)𝗂𝗇x=:=y;x{\mathsf{let}\,y\,=\,\mathsf{bernoulli}(0.4)\,\mathsf{in}\,{x\mathrel{\scalebox{0.4}[1]{${=}$}{:}{\scalebox{0.4}[1]{${=}$}}}y;x}}

the normalizing constant is either 0.40.4 or 0.60.6 depending on the value of xx. If we normalize regardless of the value of xx, then the meaning of the program must change, because it would simply return xx, and the context

𝗅𝖾𝗍​x=𝖻𝖾𝗋𝗇𝗈𝗎𝗅𝗅𝗂⁡(0.4)​𝗂𝗇​[−]\mathsf{let}\,x\,=\,\mathsf{bernoulli}(0.4)\,\mathsf{in}\,{[-]}

distinguishes this.

There is nonetheless some normalization that can be done in straight-line programs, since e.g. the meaning is not changed by prefixing a program with a closed program. It is for example safe to regard program (31) as equivalent to

(32) 𝗅𝖾𝗍z=𝖻𝖾𝗋𝗇𝗈𝗎𝗅𝗅𝗂(0.2)𝗂𝗇z=:=false;𝗅𝖾𝗍y=𝖻𝖾𝗋𝗇𝗈𝗎𝗅𝗅𝗂(0.4)𝗂𝗇x=:=y;x\mathsf{let}\,z\,=\,\mathsf{bernoulli}(0.2)\,\mathsf{in}\,{z\mathrel{\scalebox{0.4}[1]{${=}$}{:}{\scalebox{0.4}[1]{${=}$}}}\mathrm{false};\mathsf{let}\,y\,=\,\mathsf{bernoulli}(0.4)\,\mathsf{in}\,{x\mathrel{\scalebox{0.4}[1]{${=}$}{:}{\scalebox{0.4}[1]{${=}$}}}y;x}}

because the difference in normalizing constant will be the same for both values of xx.

Semantically, the interpretation of a program with free variables is a stochastic kernel, and one involving rejection too is a substochastic kernel (Definition 3.5). As we show, we can accommodate multiplication by a constant if it is uniform across all arguments; this is what we call ‘projectivized’ substochastic kernels, by analogy with the construction of a projective space from a vector space.

Definition 6.3.

The CD-category 𝖥𝗂𝗇𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗃𝖲𝗍𝗈𝖼𝗁\mathsf{FinProjStoch} of projectivized substochastic kernels is a quotient of the CD-category of 𝖥𝗂𝗇𝖲𝗎𝖻𝖲𝗍𝗈𝖼𝗁\mathsf{FinSubStoch} of substochastic maps:

  1. (1)

    objects are finite sets XX

  2. (2)

    morphisms X→YX\to Y are equivalence classes [p][p] of substochastic kernels p⁡(y|x)p(y|x) up to a scalar. That is we identify pp and qq if there exists a number λ>0\lambda>0 such that p⁡(y|x)=λ⋅q⁡(y|x)p(y|x)=\lambda\cdot q(y|x) for all x∈X,y∈Yx\in X,y\in Y. In this circumstance we write p∝qp\propto q.

It is routine to verify that the monoidal and CD category structure are preserved by this quotient.

Theorem 6.4.

The CD-categories 𝖢𝗈𝗇𝖽⁡(𝖥𝗂𝗇𝖲𝗍𝗈𝖼𝗁)\mathsf{Cond}(\mathsf{FinStoch}) and 𝖥𝗂𝗇𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗃𝖲𝗍𝗈𝖼𝗁\mathsf{FinProjStoch} are equivalent.

Proof.

Sketch. Given a conditioning channel Q:X↝YQ:X\leadsto Y presented by a finite set of observations KK, a probability kernel q⁡(y,k|x)q(y,k|x) and an observation k0∈Kk_{0}\in K, we associate to it the subprobability kernel ρQ:X→D≤1​(Y)\rho_{Q}:X\to D_{\leq 1}(Y) given by the likelihood function

ρQ​(y|x)=q⁡(y,k0|x)\rho_{Q}(y|x)=q(y,k_{0}|x)

Conversely, we associate to every subprobability kernel ρ:X→D≤1​(Y)\rho:X\to D_{\leq 1}(Y) a conditioning channel Qρ=({0,1},qρ,1)Q_{\rho}=(\{0,1\},q_{\rho},1) with a single boolean observation b:= 1b{:}\scalebox{0.5}[1]{${=}$}\,1, defined as

qρ​(y,b|x)=b⋅ρ⁡(y|x)+(1−b)⋅(1−ρ⁡(y|x)).q_{\rho}(y,b|x)=b\cdot\rho(y|x)+(1-b)\cdot(1-\rho(y|x)).

We recover the subprobability kernel ρQ\rho_{Q} from the conditioning channel QQ that way: Given any distribution p⁡(x)p(x), the posterior in Proposition 5.7 is given by

p⁡(x)​q​(y,k0|x)∑x,yp⁡(x)​q​(y,k0|x)\frac{p(x)q(y,k_{0}|x)}{\sum_{x,y}p(x)q(y,k_{0}|x)}

We see that qρq_{\rho} computes the same posterior, namely

p⁡(x)​qρ​(y,1|x)∑x,yp⁡(x)​qρ​(y,1|x)=p⁡(x)​ρ​(y|x)∑x,yp⁡(x)​ρ​(y|x)=p⁡(x)​q​(y,k0|x)∑x,yp⁡(x)​ρ​(y,k0|x)\frac{p(x)q_{\rho}(y,1|x)}{\sum_{x,y}p(x)q_{\rho}(y,1|x)}=\frac{p(x)\rho(y|x)}{\sum_{x,y}p(x)\rho(y|x)}=\frac{p(x)q(y,k_{0}|x)}{\sum_{x,y}p(x)\rho(y,k_{0}|x)}

On the other hand, the subprobability kernel ρ\rho can be recovered from QρQ_{\rho} up to a constant. For a uniform prior p⁡(x)=1/|X|p(x)=1/|X|, the posterior under QρQ_{\rho} in Proposition 5.7 becomes

ρ⁡(y|x)∑x,yρ⁡(x,y)\frac{\rho(y|x)}{\sum_{x,y}\rho(x,y)}

from which we can read off ρ⁡(y|x)\rho(y|x) up to the constant in the denominator. ∎

Identifying scalar multiples is necessary because the Cond construction by definition ‘normalizes automatically’. That is, it considers two conditioning channels equivalent if they compute the same posterior distributions for all priors. We will explore the relationship with model evidence and branching in Section 6.3.

We briefly showcase some of the structure of this category, by characterizing the discardable morphisms, and observing that conditioning gives a commutative monoid structure. The latter gives a characterization for the finite uniform distributions as units for conditioning.

Example 6.5.

A projectivized subprobability kernel p:X→Yp:X\to Y is discardable (Definition 3.2) if and only if there exists a constant λ≠0\lambda\neq 0 such that

∀x,∑yp⁡(y|x)=λ\forall x,\sum_{y}p(y|x)=\lambda

As an instance of Proposition 5.11, in particular, to give a state in 𝖥𝗂𝗇𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗃𝖲𝗍𝗈𝖼𝗁⁡(1,Y)\mathsf{FinProjStoch}(1,Y) is to give either a normalizable distribution p∈𝖥𝗂𝗇𝖲𝗍𝗈𝖼𝗁⁡(1,Y)p\in\mathsf{FinStoch}(1,Y) or the failure kernel ⊥Y=0\bot_{Y}=0.

Definition 6.6 (Conditioning product).

In 𝖢𝗈𝗇𝖽⁡(𝖥𝗂𝗇𝖲𝗍𝗈𝖼𝗁)\mathsf{Cond}(\mathsf{FinStoch}), we define an exact conditioning operation x=:=yx\mathrel{\scalebox{0.4}[1]{${=}$}{:}{\scalebox{0.4}[1]{${=}$}}}y by exactly observing true\mathrm{true} from the boolean equality test (x==y)(x==y). We define a morphism ∙:X×X↝X\bullet:X\times X\leadsto X by

x∙y=def(x=:=y);xx\bullet y\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{def}}}{{=}}(x\mathrel{\scalebox{0.4}[1]{${=}$}{:}{\scalebox{0.4}[1]{${=}$}}}y);x

In terms of projectivized subprobability kernels, this is

∙(z|x,y)={1z=x=y0otherwise\bullet(z|x,y)=\begin{cases}1&z=x=y\\ 0&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}

We call ∙\bullet the conditioning product.

Concretely for subdistributions p⁡(x),q⁡(x)p(x),q(x), the subdistribution (p∙q)(p\bullet q) has the product of mass functions

(p∙q)​(x)=p⁡(x)⋅q⁡(x)(p\bullet q)(x)=p(x)\cdot q(x)
Proposition 6.7.

The conditioning product defines a commutative monoid structure on XX, where the unit is given by the uniform distribution uX:1↝Xu_{X}:1\leadsto X.

Proof.

The operation ∙\bullet is commutative and associative already in 𝖥𝗂𝗇𝖲𝗎𝖻𝖲𝗍𝗈𝖼𝗁\mathsf{FinSubStoch}, however it does not have a unit. Conditioning with the uniform distribution produces a global factor of 1/|X|1/|X|, which is cancelled by the proportionality relation. Therefore, uXu_{X} is a unit for ∙\bullet in 𝖢𝗈𝗇𝖽⁡(𝖥𝗂𝗇𝖲𝗍𝗈𝖼𝗁)\mathsf{Cond}(\mathsf{FinStoch}). ∎

This is intuitive in programming terms: Observing from a uniform distribution gives no new information. Such a conditioning statement can thus be discarded.

Aside on non-determinism

We show the analogous version of Theorem 6.4 for nondeterminism. The Cond construction here does nothing more than add the possibility for failure (zero outputs) in a systematic way.

Proposition 6.8.

𝖢𝗈𝗇𝖽⁡(𝖱𝖾𝗅+)≅𝖱𝖾𝗅\mathsf{Cond}(\mathsf{Rel}^{+})\cong\mathsf{Rel}.

Proof.

Given a conditioning channel (K,R,k0)(K,R,k_{0}) with R⊆X×Y×KR\subseteq X\times Y\times K left-total in XX, we define a possibly non-total relation R′⊆X×YR^{\prime}\subseteq X\times Y by R′={(x,y):(x,y,k0)∈R}R^{\prime}=\{(x,y):(x,y,k_{0})\in R\}. On the other hand, given R′R^{\prime}, we form the conditioning channel (2,R′′,1)(2,R^{\prime\prime},1) with left-total relation R′′⊆X×Y×2R^{\prime\prime}\subseteq X\times Y\times 2 defined as

(x,y,b)∈R′′⇔def((x,y)∈R′⇔(b=1))(x,y,b)\in R^{\prime\prime}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{def}}}{{\Leftrightarrow}}((x,y)\in R^{\prime}\Leftrightarrow(b=1))

These constructions are easily seen to be inverses. Any relation R′R^{\prime} is recovered from R′′R^{\prime\prime} and we have (K,R,k0)≈(2,R′′,1)(K,R,k_{0})\approx(2,R^{\prime\prime},1) because Proposition 5.7 boils down to checking that (x,y,k0)∈R⇔(x,y,1)∈R′′(x,y,k_{0})\in R\Leftrightarrow(x,y,1)\in R^{\prime\prime}. ∎

The conditioning product ∙\bullet in 𝖱𝖾𝗅\mathsf{Rel} is the relation {(x,x,x):x∈X}\{(x,x,x):x\in X\}, and on states we have R∙S=R∩SR\bullet S=R\cap S. The conditioning product has a unit vX:1→Xv_{X}:1\to X given by the maximal subset vX=Xv_{X}=X.

6.3. Automatic Normalization and Straight-line Inference

By automatic normalization we mean that two (open) probabilistic programs which differ by an overall normalization constant ZZ are considered equivalent, as formalized in Section 6.2. As a consequence, the precise value of the normalization constant cannot be extracted operationally from such programs, which is a limitation whenever ZZ is itself a quantity of interest. On the other hand, auto-normalization is a convenient optimization, as seen in (32) or Proposition 6.7.

In this section, we argue that validity of auto-normalization is tied to the form of branching available in language under consideration. We distinguish straight-line inference programs with a static structure of conditions from programs where we can dynamically choose whether to execute conditions or not. This is sufficient for inference in Bayesian networks, in which the observed nodes are determined statically. For example, the Bayesian network depicted in (4) corresponds to the straight-line program in Figure 1(c). Auto-normalization is valid for straight-line programs but not for those with more general branching. The quotient from Section 6.2 arises naturally from studying contextual equivalence of a straight-line inference language. In semantical terms, this means 𝖢𝗈𝗇𝖽⁡(𝖥𝗂𝗇𝖲𝗍𝗈𝖼𝗁)\mathsf{Cond}(\mathsf{FinStoch}) does not have coproducts.

We consider the CD-calculus (Section 3.3) with base types XX for all finite sets and function symbols f¯\underline{f} for all subprobability kernels f:X→D≤1​(Y)f:X\to D_{\leq 1}(Y):

t::=x​|()|​(t,t)​|πi​t|​f¯​(t)|𝗅𝖾𝗍​x=t1​𝗂𝗇​t2\displaystyle t::=x\,|\,()\,|\,(t,t)\,|\,\pi_{i}t\,|\,\underline{f}(t)\,|\,\mathsf{let}\,x\,=\,t_{1}\,\mathsf{in}\,t_{2}

This language can express scoring and exact conditioning because there exist suitable subprobability kernels

𝗌𝖼𝗈𝗋𝖾p∈D≤1(1) and (=:=):X×X→D≤1(1)\mathsf{score}_{p}\in D_{\leq 1}(1)\text{ and }(\mathrel{\scalebox{0.4}[1]{${=}$}{:}{\scalebox{0.4}[1]{${=}$}}}):X\times X\to D_{\leq 1}(1)

We denote the this calculus 𝐏𝐒𝐋\mathbf{PSL}, for straight-line inference. Following the development in Section 3.13, the language 𝐏𝐒𝐋\mathbf{PSL} has canonical denotational semantics in 𝖥𝗂𝗇𝖲𝗎𝖻𝖲𝗍𝗈𝖼𝗁\mathsf{FinSubStoch}. (In fact, 𝐏𝐒𝐋\mathbf{PSL} is precisely the internal language of 𝖥𝗂𝗇𝖲𝗎𝖻𝖲𝗍𝗈𝖼𝗁\mathsf{FinSubStoch} as a CD category.)

We also consider a richer language, 𝐏\mathbf{P}, which contains the syntax of 𝐏𝐒𝐋\mathbf{PSL} and also if-then-else branching:

t::=…|𝗂𝖿​t1​𝗍𝗁𝖾𝗇​t2​𝖾𝗅𝗌𝖾​t3t::=\dots\,|\,\mathsf{if}~t_{1}~\mathsf{then}~t_{2}~\mathsf{else}~t_{3}

with typing rule

Γ⊢t1:2Γ⊢t2:AΓ⊢t3:AΓ⊢𝗂𝖿​t1​𝗍𝗁𝖾𝗇​t2​𝖾𝗅𝗌𝖾​t3:A‾\Gamma\vdash\mathsf{if}~t_{1}~\mathsf{then}~t_{2}~\mathsf{else}~t_{3}:A\Gamma\vdash t_{1}:2\quad\Gamma\vdash t_{2}:A\quad\Gamma\vdash t_{3}:A

This language can also be interpreted in 𝖥𝗂𝗇𝖲𝗎𝖻𝖲𝗍𝗈𝖼𝗁\mathsf{FinSubStoch}, via

⟦𝗂𝖿​t1​𝗍𝗁𝖾𝗇​t2​𝖾𝗅𝗌𝖾​t3⟧​(a|γ)=⟦t2⟧​(a|γ)⋅⟦t1⟧​(true|γ)+⟦t3⟧​(a|γ)⋅⟦t1⟧​(false|γ){\llbracket\mathsf{if}~t_{1}~\mathsf{then}~t_{2}~\mathsf{else}~t_{3}\rrbracket}(a|\gamma)={\llbracket t_{2}\rrbracket}(a|\gamma)\cdot{\llbracket t_{1}\rrbracket}(\mathrm{true}|\gamma)+{\llbracket t_{3}\rrbracket}(a|\gamma)\cdot{\llbracket t_{1}\rrbracket}(\mathrm{false}|\gamma)

Categorically, this makes use of the distributive coproducts in 𝖥𝗂𝗇𝖲𝗎𝖻𝖲𝗍𝗈𝖼𝗁\mathsf{FinSubStoch} (38, 45). 𝐏\mathbf{P} is a commonly considered probabilistic language, and subprobability kernel semantics are already known to be fully abstract, though we rederive this here.

As explained in the introduction to this section, a program in the language 𝐏\mathbf{P} or 𝐏𝐒𝐋\mathbf{PSL} is typically executed by some sort of inference engine, which tries to sample (usually approximately) from the posterior distribution it defines. In the semantics, we express this top-level normalization for a finite set XX using the function 𝗇𝗈𝗋𝗆𝖺𝗅𝗂𝗓𝖾:D≤1​(X)→D≤1​(X)\mathsf{normalize}:D_{\leq 1}(X)\to D_{\leq 1}(X) which is defined as

𝗇𝗈𝗋𝗆𝖺𝗅𝗂𝗓𝖾⁡(φ)​(x)={1Z⋅φ⁡(x)where ​Z=∑x∈Xφ⁡(x)≠00where ​∀x.φ⁡(x)=0\mathsf{normalize}(\varphi)(x)=\begin{cases}\tfrac{1}{Z}\cdot\varphi(x)&\text{where }Z=\sum_{x\in X}\varphi(x)\neq 0\\ 0&\text{where }\forall x.\,\varphi(x)=0\end{cases}

The zero distribution is mapped to itself, signaling failure of normalization.

Definition 6.9.

Two closed 𝐏\mathbf{P} programs s,t:Xs,t:X are called observationally equivalent, written s≈ts\approx t, if the normalized distributions they define are equal, that is 𝗇𝗈𝗋𝗆𝖺𝗅𝗂𝗓𝖾⁡(⟦s⟧)=𝗇𝗈𝗋𝗆𝖺𝗅𝗂𝗓𝖾⁡(⟦t⟧)\mathsf{normalize}({\llbracket s\rrbracket})=\mathsf{normalize}({\llbracket t\rrbracket}).

We say that two open programs Γ⊢s,t:X\Gamma\vdash s,t:X are contextually equivalent if under every closed context C⁡[−]C[-] we have C⁡[s]≈C⁡[t]C[s]\approx C[t]. The distinguishing power crucially depends on the fragment of the language we are allowed to use in the contexts C⁡[−]C[-].

Definition 6.10.

The terms s,ts,t are called straight-line equivalent, written s≈𝐏𝐒𝐋ts\approx_{\mathbf{PSL}}t, if for every closed context C⁡[−]C[-] in 𝐏𝐒𝐋\mathbf{PSL} (without branching), we have C⁡[s]≈C⁡[t]C[s]\approx C[t]. The terms s,ts,t are called branching equivalent, written s≈𝐏ts\approx_{\mathbf{P}}t, if for every closed context C⁡[−]C[-] in 𝐏\mathbf{P} (possibly involving branching), we have C⁡[s]≈C⁡[t]C[s]\approx C[t].

The following proposition shows that straight-line equivalence can distinguish subprobability kernels up to a constant.

Proposition 6.11.

Two open programs are straight-line equivalent iff their denotations are proportional.

s≈𝐏𝐒𝐋t⇔⟦s⟧∝⟦t⟧s\approx_{\mathbf{PSL}}t\Leftrightarrow{\llbracket s\rrbracket}\propto{\llbracket t\rrbracket}

That is 𝖥𝗂𝗇𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗃𝖲𝗍𝗈𝖼𝗁\mathsf{FinProjStoch} is fully abstract for the language 𝐏𝐒𝐋\mathbf{PSL}.

Proof.

⇐\Leftarrow Is is easy to show that the semantics of all 𝐏𝐒𝐋\mathbf{PSL} constructs are linear or bilinear and hence respect the relation ∝\propto. ⇒\Rightarrow Let s≈𝐏𝐒𝐋ts\approx_{\mathbf{PSL}}t and consider the straight-line context

C⁡[t]=def𝗅𝖾𝗍​x=uX​𝗂𝗇​(x,t)C[t]\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{def}}}{{=}}\mathsf{let}\,x\,=\,u_{X}\,\mathsf{in}\,(x,t)

where again uXu_{X} denotes the uniform distribution on the finite set XX. Its denotation is

⟦C⁡[t]⟧​(x,y)=1|X|​⟦t⟧​(y|x){\llbracket C[t]\rrbracket}(x,y)=\frac{1}{|X|}{\llbracket t\rrbracket}(y|x)

By assumption ⟦C⁡[s]⟧∝⟦C⁡[t]⟧{\llbracket C[s]\rrbracket}\propto{\llbracket C[t]\rrbracket}, so we have ⟦s⟧∝⟦t⟧{\llbracket s\rrbracket}\propto{\llbracket t\rrbracket}. ∎

This gives a clear interpretation of Theorem 6.4. In our current terminology, the Cond construction aims to give a canonical semantics for straight-line inference programs: the construction presents a normal form for straight-line programs up to straight-line equivalence. The lack of branching is reflected in the fact that unlike 𝖥𝗂𝗇𝖲𝗎𝖻𝖲𝗍𝗈𝖼𝗁\mathsf{FinSubStoch}, 𝖥𝗂𝗇𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗃𝖲𝗍𝗈𝖼𝗁\mathsf{FinProjStoch} does not have coproducts.

Branching inference

Up to straight-line equivalence, programs which differ by a global constant are not distinguishable, that is auto-normalization is valid. This changes if we allow branching in the contexts, because branching can be used to extract the normalization constant. This trick is fundamental to so-called ‘Bayesian model selection’. If yy is a closed program, then the boolean program

𝗂𝖿​𝖻𝖾𝗋𝗇𝗈𝗎𝗅𝗅𝗂​(0.5)​𝗍𝗁𝖾𝗇​y;true​𝖾𝗅𝗌𝖾​false\mathsf{if}~\mathsf{bernoulli(0.5)}~\mathsf{then}~y;\mathrm{true}~\mathsf{else}~\mathrm{false}

normalizes to a distribution which returns true\mathrm{true} with probability

p=0.5⋅Z0.5⋅Z+0.5=ZZ+1 where ​Z=∑x⟦y⟧​(x)p=\frac{0.5\cdot Z}{0.5\cdot Z+0.5}=\frac{Z}{Z+1}\qquad\text{ where }Z=\sum_{x}{\llbracket y\rrbracket}(x)

and false\mathrm{false} with probability 1Z+1\frac{1}{Z+1}. Because the assignment Z↦Z/(Z+1)Z\mapsto Z/(Z+1) is a bijection [0,∞)→[0,1)[0,\infty)\to[0,1), we can recover ZZ from the probability pp. It follows that 𝖥𝗂𝗇𝖲𝗎𝖻𝖲𝗍𝗈𝖼𝗁\mathsf{FinSubStoch} is fully abstract for 𝐏\mathbf{P}.

Proposition 6.12.

Two open programs s,ts,t are branching equivalent if their denotations are equal as subprobability kernels.

s≈𝐏t⇔⟦s⟧=⟦t⟧:⟦Γ⟧→D≤1(⟦X⟧)s\approx_{\mathbf{P}}t\Leftrightarrow{\llbracket s\rrbracket}={\llbracket t\rrbracket}:{\llbracket\Gamma\rrbracket}\to D_{\leq 1}({\llbracket X\rrbracket})

That is 𝖥𝗂𝗇𝖲𝗎𝖻𝖲𝗍𝗈𝖼𝗁\mathsf{FinSubStoch} is fully abstract for the language 𝐏\mathbf{P}.

Proof.

From straight-line equivalence, we know that ⟦s⟧=λ⋅⟦t⟧{\llbracket s\rrbracket}=\lambda\cdot{\llbracket t\rrbracket}. We then use the ‘Bayesian model selection’ trick to show λ=1\lambda=1. ∎

The tradeoff between straight-line inference and branching inference is an interesting design decision: Branching inference is more general and allows us to extract the normalization constant. On the other hand, restricting ourselves to straight-line inference, we are free to normalize at any point, which leads to an appealing equational theory. For example, an ‘uninformative’ observation form a uniform distribution can be eliminated (Proposition 6.7).

We emphasize that the crucial difference between 𝐏𝐒𝐋\mathbf{PSL} and 𝐏\mathbf{P} lies in putting conditions in branches. Even in 𝐏𝐒𝐋\mathbf{PSL}, we can still implement if-then-else when the branches do not involve conditions, because we can make use of the probability kernel

𝗂𝗍𝖾:2×X×X→D⁡(X)\mathsf{ite}:2\times X\times X\to D(X)

with 𝗂𝗍𝖾⁡(1,x,y)=δx\mathsf{ite}(1,x,y)=\delta_{x} and 𝗂𝗍𝖾⁡(0,x,y)=δy\mathsf{ite}(0,x,y)=\delta_{y}. If t1,t2t_{1},t_{2} are discardable (condition-free) terms, we can define

(𝗂𝖿​c​𝗍𝗁𝖾𝗇​t1​𝖾𝗅𝗌𝖾​t2)=def𝗂𝗍𝖾⁡(c,t1,t2).(\mathsf{if}~c~\mathsf{then}~t_{1}~\mathsf{else}~t_{2})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{def}}}{{=}}\mathsf{ite}(c,t_{1},t_{2}).

In 𝐏𝐒𝐋\mathbf{PSL}, the structure of conditions is static, while it is dynamic in 𝐏\mathbf{P}.

7. Context, Related Work and Outlook

7.1. Symbolic Disintegration, Consistency and Paradoxes

Our line of work can be regarded as a synthetic and axiomatic counterpart of the symbolic disintegration of (42) (see also (15, 36, 37, 51)). That work provides in particular verified program transformations to convert an arbitrary probabilistic program of type 𝖱⊗τ\mathsf{R}\otimes\tau to an equivalent one that is of the form

𝗅𝖾𝗍​x=lebesgue⁡()​𝗂𝗇​𝗅𝖾𝗍​y=M​𝗂𝗇​(x,y)\mathsf{let}\,x\,=\,\mathrm{lebesgue}()\,\mathsf{in}\,{\mathsf{let}\,y\,=\,M\,\mathsf{in}\,{(x,y)}}

Now the exact conditioning x:=ox{:}\scalebox{0.5}[1]{${=}$}\,o can be carried out by substituting oo for xx in MM. We emphasize the similarity to our treatment of inference problems in Section 3, as well as the role that coordinate transformations play in both our work (49) and (42). One language novelty in our work is that exact conditioning is a first-class construct in our language, as opposed to a whole-program transformation, which makes the consistency of exact conditioning more apparent.

Consistency is a fundamental concern for exact conditioning. Borel’s paradox is an example of an inconsistency that arises if one is careless with exact conditioning ((26, Ch. 15), (25, §3.3)): It arises when naively substituting equivalent equations within (=:=)(\mathrel{\scalebox{0.4}[1]{${=}$}{:}{\scalebox{0.4}[1]{${=}$}}}). For example, the equation x−y=0x-y=0 is equivalent to x/y=1x/y=1 over the (nonzero) real numbers. Yet, in a hypothetical extension of our language which allows division, the following programs would not contextually equivalent, as discussed in Example 2.2:

x = normal(0,1)y = normal(0,1)x-y =:= 0≢x = normal(0,1)y = normal(0,1)x/y =:= 1{{{{{{\begin{array}[]{l}\text{\lstinline{{\lst@@@set@language\lst@@@set@numbers\lst@@@set@frame\lst@@@set@rulecolor\lst@@@set@frame\lst@@@set@language{\@listingGroup{ltx_lst_identifier}{{x}}}{\@listingGroup{ltx_lst_space}{ }}={\@listingGroup{ltx_lst_space}{ }}{\@listingGroup{ltx_lst_emph}{\color[rgb]{0.6,0,0}{normal}}}(0,1)}}}}\\ \text{\lstinline{{\lst@@@set@language\lst@@@set@numbers\lst@@@set@frame\lst@@@set@rulecolor\lst@@@set@frame\lst@@@set@language{\@listingGroup{ltx_lst_identifier}{{y}}}{\@listingGroup{ltx_lst_space}{ }}={\@listingGroup{ltx_lst_space}{ }}{\@listingGroup{ltx_lst_emph}{\color[rgb]{0.6,0,0}{normal}}}(0,1)}}}}\\ \text{\lstinline{{\lst@@@set@language\lst@@@set@numbers\lst@@@set@frame\lst@@@set@rulecolor\lst@@@set@frame\lst@@@set@language{\@listingGroup{ltx_lst_identifier}{{x}}}-{\@listingGroup{ltx_lst_identifier}{{y}}}{\@listingGroup{ltx_lst_space}{ }}=:={\@listingGroup{ltx_lst_space}{ }}0}}}}\\ \end{array}\not\equiv\begin{array}[]{l}\text{\lstinline{{\lst@@@set@language\lst@@@set@numbers\lst@@@set@frame\lst@@@set@rulecolor\lst@@@set@frame\lst@@@set@language{\@listingGroup{ltx_lst_identifier}{{x}}}{\@listingGroup{ltx_lst_space}{ }}={\@listingGroup{ltx_lst_space}{ }}{\@listingGroup{ltx_lst_emph}{\color[rgb]{0.6,0,0}{normal}}}(0,1)}}}}\\ \text{\lstinline{{\lst@@@set@language\lst@@@set@numbers\lst@@@set@frame\lst@@@set@rulecolor\lst@@@set@frame\lst@@@set@language{\@listingGroup{ltx_lst_identifier}{{y}}}{\@listingGroup{ltx_lst_space}{ }}={\@listingGroup{ltx_lst_space}{ }}{\@listingGroup{ltx_lst_emph}{\color[rgb]{0.6,0,0}{normal}}}(0,1)}}}}\\ \text{\lstinline{{\lst@@@set@language\lst@@@set@numbers\lst@@@set@frame\lst@@@set@rulecolor\lst@@@set@frame\lst@@@set@language{\@listingGroup{ltx_lst_identifier}{{x}}}/{\@listingGroup{ltx_lst_identifier}{{y}}}{\@listingGroup{ltx_lst_space}{ }}=:={\@listingGroup{ltx_lst_space}{ }}1}}}}\end{array}

For that reason, we make it clear in our treatment of inference problems (Section 4.3) that conditioning on a deterministic observation (:=)({:}\scalebox{0.5}[1]{${=}$}\,) is the fundamental notion. Binary conditioning (=:=)(\mathrel{\scalebox{0.4}[1]{${=}$}{:}{\scalebox{0.4}[1]{${=}$}}}) is a derived notion which involves further choices, and those choices are not equivalent. Our approach also makes it clear that we should always condition on random variables directly, and not on (boolean) predicates: By presenting conditioning as an algebraic effect, the expressions (s=:=t):𝖨(s\mathrel{\scalebox{0.4}[1]{${=}$}{:}{\scalebox{0.4}[1]{${=}$}}}t):\mathsf{I} and (s==t):bool(s==t):\mathrm{bool} have a different formal status and can no longer be confused.

7.2. Contextual Equivalence for Exact Conditioning languages

In this article, we have emphasized the role of program equations for manipulating probabilistic programs, and based the Cond construction on an analysis of contextual equivalence of straight-line inference (Section 6).

While we have fully characterized the case of finite probability (Section 6.2), a corresponding explict characterization of contextual equivalence for the Gaussian language is still outstanding. We have given partial results in that direction (see (49)) in the form of a sound equational theory for contextual equivalence. The classification of effects n→0n\to 0 in 𝖢𝗈𝗇𝖽⁡(𝖦𝖺𝗎𝗌𝗌)\mathsf{Cond}(\mathsf{Gauss}) is not straightforward: it is not true that every effect is observing from a unique distribution 0→n0\to n, as for example (=:=):2→0(\mathrel{\scalebox{0.4}[1]{${=}$}{:}{\scalebox{0.4}[1]{${=}$}}}):2\to 0 is not of that form. We believe that by passing to an extension category of Gaussians 𝖦𝖺𝗎𝗌𝗌→𝖦𝖺𝗎𝗌𝗌𝖤𝗑\mathsf{Gauss}\to\mathsf{GaussEx}, we can obtain the desired duality and achieve a more explicit characterization.

It is a further challenge to find semantics for exact conditioning with branching. Automatic normalization is no longer valid here (Section 6.3) and the subtleties of (25) have to be accounted for. Mathematically, this would be an extension of the Cond construction which produces a distributive Freyd category (38). An example of a categorical model of the Beta-Bernoulli process with branching (but no first-class conditioning) is in (46).

7.3. Other Directions

Categorical tools

Once a foundation is in algebraic or categorical form, it is easy to make connections to and draw inspiration from a variety of other work: The 𝖮𝖻𝗌\mathsf{Obs} construction (Definition 5.1) that we considered here is reminiscent of lenses (7) and the Oles construction (20). These have recently been applied to probability theory (43), quantum theory (22) and reversible computing (21). The details and intuitions are different, but a deeper connection or generalization may be profitable in the future.

Probabilistic logic programming

The concept of exact conditioning is reminiscent of unification in Prolog-style logic programming. Our presentation in (49) is partly inspired by the algebraic presentation of predicate logic of (44), which has a similar signature and axioms. Logic programming is also closely related to relational programming, and we note that our laws for conditioning are reminiscent of graphical presentations of categories of linear relations (1, 4, 3).

ProbLog (8) supports both logic variables as well as random variables within a common formalism. We have not considered logic variables in conjunction with the Gaussian language, but a challenge for future work is to bring the ideas of exact conditioning closer to the ideas of unification, both practically and in terms of the semantics. This is again related to the extension 𝖦𝖺𝗎𝗌𝗌𝖤𝗑\mathsf{GaussEx} by “improper priors”, which are a unit for the conditioning product in the same way uniform distributions are in finite probability (Proposition 6.7). The connections with logic programming are spelled out in more detail in (48, Section 20.2).

Implementation

The purpose of our Gaussian language was to give a minimalistic calculus in which to study the novel effect of conditioning in isolation. The close fit of the denotational semantics to the language was thus expected, and can be seen as an instance of letting semantics inspire language design. To extend our calculus to a full-blown programming language, one can make use of the general framework of algebraic effects to combine conditioning with other effects like memory or recursion. For example, we can treat higher-order functions by modelling the language on a presheaf category, which is cartesian closed. The operational semantics easily extend to a full language, for which we have given implementations in Python and F# (47).

8. Appendix

8.1. Overview of Measure Theory

In order to formalize probability distributions with uncountable support such as Gaussians, one traditionally employs measure theory. While measure theory is not central to the understanding of this article, it is needed to make certain arguments and intuitions rigorous, so we provide a short reference and refer to (28) for a comprehensive introduction.

Measurable spaces

A σ\sigma-algebra on a set XX is a collection of subsets of XX which contains ∅\emptyset and is closed under complementation and countable union. A measurable space is a pair (X,ΣX)(X,\Sigma_{X}) of a set XX and a σ\sigma-algebra ΣX\Sigma_{X} on XX. The subsets U∈ΣXU\in\Sigma_{X} are called measurable subsets. A function f:X→Yf:X\to Y between measurable spaces is called measurable if for all measurable subsets A⊆YA\subseteq Y, the preimage f−1​(A)f^{-1}(A) is measurable in XX. The product space X×YX\times Y is naturally equipped with the product-σ\sigma-algebra, which is generated by the rectangles A×BA\times B for A∈ΣX,B∈ΣYA\in\Sigma_{X},B\in\Sigma_{Y}.

Every topological space XX comes with a natural σ\sigma-algebra, namely the Borel σ\sigma-algebra ℬ⁡(X)\mathcal{B}(X) generated by its open sets. Continuous functions between topological spaces become measurable under this definition.

All examples of measurable spaces in this article will be of a particularly well-behaved type, namely standard Borel spaces.

Definition 8.1.

A Polish space is a topological space homeomorphic to a complete metric space with a countable dense subset. A standard Borel space is a measurable space which is isomorphic to (X,ℬ⁡(X))(X,\mathcal{B}(X)) for some Polish space XX.

We write 𝖲𝖻𝗌\mathsf{Sbs} for the category of standard Borel spaces and measurable maps. This category includes all spaces that will be relevant for real-valued probability, for example ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, the interval [0,1][0,1] and countable discrete spaces.

Definition 8.2.

Let XX be a measurable space. A measure on XX is a function μ:ΣX→[0,∞]\mu:\Sigma_{X}\to[0,\infty] such that

(33) μ⁡(∅)=0 and μ⁡(∑i=1∞Ai)=∑i=1∞μ⁡(Ai)\mu(\emptyset)=0\qquad\text{ and }\qquad\mu\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}A_{i}\right)=\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\mu(A_{i})

where ∑iAi\sum_{i}A_{i} denotes disjoint union.

A probability measure is a measure satisfying μ⁡(X)=1\mu(X)=1. If μ\mu is a measure on XX and f:X→Yf:X\to Y is measurable, the pushforward measure f∗​μf_{*}\mu is defined by f∗​μ​(A)=μ⁡(f−1​(A))f_{*}\mu(A)=\mu(f^{-1}(A)). For x∈Xx\in X, the Dirac measure δx\delta_{x} is the probability measure on XX defined, using Iverson backet notation, by δx(A)=[x∈A]\delta_{x}(A)=[x\in A]. The Borel-Lebesgue measure is the unique measure on (ℝ,ℬ⁡(ℝ))(\mathbb{R},\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})) assigning every interval its length, that is ℓ⁡([a,b])=b−a\ell([a,b])=b-a for all a≤ba\leq b. For two probability measures μ,ν\mu,\nu, the product probability measure μ⊗ν\mu\otimes\nu is uniquely defined via (μ⊗ν)​(A×B)=μ⁡(A)⋅ν⁡(B)(\mu\otimes\nu)(A\times B)=\mu(A)\cdot\nu(B) for all measurable A,BA,B. A subset which is assigned measure zero can be seen as negligible; this informs the following terminology:

Definition 8.3.

If μ\mu is a measure on XX and ϕ⁡(x)\phi(x) some measurable property, we say ϕ\phi holds μ\mu-almost everywhere if μ⁡({x∈X:¬ϕ⁡(x)})=0\mu(\{x\in X:\neg\phi(x)\})=0. We say μ\mu is absolutely continuous with respect to ν\nu, written μ≪ν\mu\ll\nu, if for all measurable sets AA, ν⁡(A)=0\nu(A)=0 implies μ⁡(A)=0\mu(A)=0.

Integration

For a nonnegative measurable function f:X→[0,∞)f:X\to[0,\infty) and a measure μ\mu, its integral is defined as

∫Xf⁡(x)​μ​(𝑑x)=defsup{Ai}∑iμ⁡(Ui)⋅infx∈Uif⁡(x)∈[0,∞]\int_{X}f(x)\mu(\mathrm{d}x)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{def}}}{{=}}\sup_{\{A_{i}\}}\sum_{i}\mu(U_{i})\cdot\inf_{x\in U_{i}}f(x)\quad\in\quad[0,\infty]

where the supremum ranges over finite measurable partitions of XX. The integral extends to measurable functions f:X→ℝf:X\to\mathbb{R} that are integrable, i.e. satisfy ∫|f⁡(x)|​μ​(𝑑x)<∞\int|f(x)|\mu(\mathrm{d}x)<\infty. Fubini’s theorem states that the order of integration can be interchanged; for all probability measures μ,ν\mu,\nu and integrable f:X×Y→ℝf:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}, we have

(34) ∫∫⁡f⁡(x,y)​μ​(𝑑x)​ν​(𝑑y)=∫∫⁡f⁡(x,y)​ν​(𝑑y)​μ​(𝑑x)\int\int f(x,y)\mu(\mathrm{d}x)\nu(\mathrm{d}y)=\int\int f(x,y)\nu(\mathrm{d}y)\mu(\mathrm{d}x)

Density functions are important practical tools for defining measures: If μ\mu is a measure on XX and f:X→[0,∞)f:X\to[0,\infty) is measurable, then

ν(A)=∫Af(x)μ(dx)=def∫f(x)[x∈A]μ(dx)\nu(A)=\int_{A}f(x)\mu(\mathrm{d}x)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{def}}}{{=}}\int f(x)[x\in A]\mu(\mathrm{d}x)

defines another measure. For example, the standard normal distribution on ℝ\mathbb{R} is defined as having the density function φ\varphi with respect to the Lebesgue measure, where

φ(x)=12​πe−x2/2\varphi(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-x^{2}/2}
Definition 8.4.

A probability kernel X↝YX\leadsto Y between measurable spaces is a function f:X×ΣY→[0,1]f:X\times\Sigma_{Y}\to[0,1] such that f⁡(−,A)f(-,A) is measurable for all A∈ΣYA\in\Sigma_{Y} and f⁡(x,−)f(x,-) is a probability measure for all x∈Xx\in X. Kernels f:X↝Yf:X\leadsto Y and g:Y↝Zg:Y\leadsto Z compose using integration

(35) (g∙f)​(x,A)=∫Yg⁡(y,A)​f​(x,𝑑y)(g\bullet f)(x,A)=\int_{Y}g(y,A)f(x,\mathrm{d}y)

and any measurable map f:X→Yf:X\to Y induces a Dirac kernel δf:X↝Y\delta_{f}:X\leadsto Y via δf(x,A)=[f(x)∈A]\delta_{f}(x,A)=[f(x)\in A].

Definition 8.5 ((11)).

The category 𝖡𝗈𝗋𝖾𝗅𝖲𝗍𝗈𝖼𝗁\mathsf{BorelStoch} consists of standard Borel spaces and probability kernels between them. Identities are given by δ𝗂𝖽X\delta_{\mathsf{id}_{X}} and composition is kernel composition.

𝖡𝗈𝗋𝖾𝗅𝖲𝗍𝗈𝖼𝗁\mathsf{BorelStoch} has the structure of a Markov category, whose tensor is given by X⊗Y=X×YX\otimes Y=X\times Y on objects and by product measures on morphisms. Copying and discarding is given by the Dirac kernels for the canonical maps Δ:X→X×X\Delta:X\to X\times X, !:X→1!:X\to 1 in 𝖲𝖻𝗌\mathsf{Sbs}.

Our example Markov categories 𝖥𝗂𝗇𝖲𝗍𝗈𝖼𝗁\mathsf{FinStoch} and 𝖦𝖺𝗎𝗌𝗌\mathsf{Gauss} faithfully embed in 𝖡𝗈𝗋𝖾𝗅𝖲𝗍𝗈𝖼𝗁\mathsf{BorelStoch}, where we interpret

  1. (1)

    the finite set XX as the discrete standard Borel space (X,𝒫⁡(X))(X,\mathcal{P}(X))

  2. (2)

    the object nn of 𝖦𝖺𝗎𝗌𝗌\mathsf{Gauss} as (ℝn,ℬ⁡(ℝn))(\mathbb{R}^{n},\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^{n}))

and the morphisms of these categories as actual probability kernels.

Definition 8.6 (Giry monad).

There is a monad 𝒢:𝖲𝖻𝗌→𝖲𝖻𝗌\mathcal{G}:\mathsf{Sbs}\to\mathsf{Sbs} due to Giry (16) that assigns to XX the space of probability measures 𝒢​X\mathcal{G}X, endowed with the least σ\sigma-algebra making all evaluations evA:𝒢​X→[0,1],μ↦μ⁡(A)\mathrm{ev}_{A}:\mathcal{G}X\to[0,1],\mu\mapsto\mu(A) measurable for A∈ΣXA\in\Sigma_{X}. The unit of this monad takes the Dirac measure x↦δxx\mapsto\delta_{x}. Kleisli composition takes the average measure via integration, that is for f:X→𝒢​Yf:X\to\mathcal{G}Y and μ∈𝒢​X\mu\in\mathcal{G}X, we have the Kleisli extension

(36) f†​(μ)​(A)=∫Xf⁡(x)​(A)​μ​(𝑑x)f^{\dagger}(\mu)(A)=\int_{X}f(x)(A)\mu(\mathrm{d}x)

For h:X→Yh:X\to Y, the functorial action 𝒢​(h)​(μ)\mathcal{G}(h)(\mu) is given by the pushforward measure h∗​μh_{*}\mu.

The Giry monad is strong, affine and commutative, where commutativity follows from Fubini’s theorem. A Kleisli arrow X→𝒢​YX\to\mathcal{G}Y is the same as a Markov kernel X↝YX\leadsto Y, and Kleisli composition (36) agrees with kernel composition (35).

8.2. CD-calculus

We verify that the remaining axioms of the CD calculus hold in any CD model, completing the proof from Section 3.5.

Proof of Proposition 3.14.

(let. ξ ) follows from the compositionality of the semantics. ( ∗ . β ), ( ∗ . η ) and ( unit . η ) are are immediate. We proceed to prove that (let.lin) is valid, that is if tt uses xx exactly once, then

We argue by induction over the term structure of tt.

Variable
